🔥🇲🇽 <u>15 years in prison for defending his forest</u>

In Oaxaca, Zapotec campesino Pablo López Alavez lost 15 years to prison on a "qualified homicide" charge invented to punish him for defending his community's forest — seized in 2010 by 15 hooded men without a warrant, sentenced in 2017 to 30 years, and freed only in 2026 when the fabricated case finally collapsed. La Jornada counts him among the environmental defenders criminalized for standing between the forest and the loggers.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>76% OF MEXICO’S CARS GO NORTH</u>

Mexico built 344,940 vehicles in August and exported 300,475 — with the US absorbing 76.3% of this year’s auto exports, some 1.7 million units, per INEGI/AMIA data. Output slipped 1.4%, the fourth monthly dip of 2026, yet domestic sales hit their highest January-August level since records began in 2005.

text:
🇲🇽🌎 <u>PUBLIC OFFICE, ONE NATIONALITY</u>

Building on Sheinbaum’s sovereignty agenda, Senator Laura Escalante of Oaxaca has introduced an initiative to require Senate candidates to hold Mexican nationality only — extending a rule already in force for the presidency, governors and mayors. “Regardless of the office, public servants must answer solely to the interests of the homeland,” the proposal reads, citing past governors accused of serving foreign interference.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>WHEN THE REAL NARCO-STATE GOT A PASS</u>

A 2013 US State Department report documented 26,121 people disappeared under Calderón (2006-2012), 7,000 unidentified bodies, and systematic torture by security forces — yet Obama imposed zero sanctions and never said “narco-government,” keeping the Mérida money flowing. Calderón’s security chief, García Luna, was later convicted in a US court of taking millions in cartel bribes while running the drug war.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>THE US KNEW SALINAS WAS NARCO-GUARDED</u>

A declassified US Embassy cable from Nov 10, 1987 states that Carlos Salinas de Gortari’s campaign security was “headed by the renowned narco-traffickers Miguel Aldana and Armando Pavón Reyes” — both linked to the 1985 murder of DEA agent Camarena; Aldana, a former Interpol Mexico chief the DEA kept a file on through 2026. A year later Salinas took the presidency and signed NAFTA — Washington backing the man its own embassy called narco-protected.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>SOVEREIGNTY, 500 METERS FROM THE US</u>

Less than 500 meters from the US border in Ciudad Juárez, President Sheinbaum told more than 15,000 people it “has cost the country many lives to be independent,” invoking Pancho Villa and pledging a desalination plant for Baja California. “Peoples without memory also lack a compass — whoever does not remember their history does not know why this moment arrived, nor where we are going.”

🚨🇲🇽 <u>THE GUNS COME FROM THE US</u>

A 22-year-old Arizona prison officer, Yanet Dowden, has been bound over for trial in a Hermosillo federal court — caught in Sonora smuggling more than 5,000 rounds of ammunition south to the Sinaloa cartel’s “La Mayiza” faction. Washington lectures Mexico about “narco-trafficking” while its own corrections officers run the bullets that arm the cartels.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>The Fed Sneezes, Wall Street Sells Mexico — Peso Has Worst Week Since March</u>

After the Fed's first rate hike since July 2023 — a quarter point, with another signaled before year-end — the peso posted its worst week since March, down 1.54% to 17.23 per dollar, while the BMV slid to 63,375 points, its lowest close since December 2025. The 'weakness' is imported: it was US monetary policy, not Mexican fundamentals, that moved the tape.

🇲🇽🚆 <u>Privatized Rail Barons Balk as Mexico Moves to Triple Their Tax</u>

The 2027 budget would raise the tax on freight-rail gross income from 1.25% to 3% — and the concessionaires who were handed the tracks in the 1990s are pushing back, insisting Mexican cargo rail is 'one of the most competitive' at 3 cents per ton-kilometer. Meanwhile Sheinbaum is laying the passenger lines those private operators let die. The rails were always public; the profits, less so.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>1989: The CIA Drew Up Plans to Invade Mexico</u>

A declassified CIA assessment — 'Mexico Outlook for the Salinas Administration,' dated May 1, 1989 and signed by director William Webster — shows Washington gamed out a 'unilateral military intervention' in Mexico, to be weighed 'in the extremely improbable case of imminent political system collapse.' The agency put 20% odds on a crisis grave enough to consider it. Trump's talk of sending troops isn't a new idea — it's a declassified one.
